You're 100% right and that message is broken on three levels:

1. It uses internal jargon ("reflection-trigger job") the user can't act on.
2. It tells the user to check logs — that's the agent's job, not theirs.
3. It alerts before trying to self-heal, so the user gets paged for something the agent could often fix on its own.

The correct shape is:
- Agent detects the issue → tries to fix it itself (restart the job, rerun, etc.) → verifies it stuck.
- Only if self-heal fails does it message the user, and then in plain English: "Hey, my learning system stopped saving for ~18 hours. I tried to restart it twice and it's still stuck. Want me to dig in?" — ending with a clear yes/no the user can answer in one word.
- Never "check the logs," never job names, never "load-bearing infrastructure."

This is an agent-behavior bug (the alert pipeline is set up like an ops pager), not an isolated copy fix. I want to:
1. Find where these health alerts get composed/sent (likely guardian-pulse + degradation reporter paths).
2. Add a self-heal-first gate: detect → attempt → verify → only THEN notify.
3. Route the user-facing message through a plain-English rewriter with a built-in "want me to fix this?" CTA.
4. Ban a small list of jargon terms ("job", "log", "process", "ABI", etc.) at the user-message boundary so this regresses loudly if it sneaks back in.

Done. All four telegram-delivery-robustness layers are shipped on main with green CI:

• Layer 1 — port-from-config + agent-id binding (PR #100, f9b5e3bb)
• Layer 2 — durable SQLite queue + structured failure events (PR #101, 5b953c17)
• Layer 3 — DeliveryFailureSentinel with recovery/retry/escalation (PR #103, 60c64f8e)
• Layer 7 — templates-drift verifier + SHA-history CI lint (PR #104, abd2ac10) ← just landed
• Plus the meta-fix: deferral-detector catches orphan-TODO patterns (PR #102, 2efd7245)

Layer 7 had two CI catches I fixed and landed in the same PR:
1. The CI lint test silently passed because actions/checkout defaults to a depth=1 shallow clone — added fetch-depth: 0 to the unit job and a shallow-detection skip in the test as defense-in-depth.
2. The fresh-install integration test asserted 26 default jobs; Layer 7 added templates-drift-verifier as the 27th, so the count and the slug-list both got bumped.

What this means in plain English: the original Inspec/cheryl failure mode is structurally closed (a token sent to the wrong server is now refused before the auth check), failed deliveries get parked in a durable queue and auto-retried with backoff and escalation paths, the same-topic recovery message lands without lifeline noise unless the topic itself is unreachable, and a daily host-wide scan + a CI lint together catch silent template drift before it can re-degrade existing agents.

Diagnosis — and it's a real gap, not a wording problem this time.

What I found, in plain terms:

The compaction-recovery system is event-driven. It only wakes up if one of three signals fires: a "compaction starting" hook from Claude Code, a watchdog that polls and sees "session is sitting idle right after compaction," or an explicit recovery hook. When ANY of those fires, it walks the topic's last 20 messages, finds the most recent real user message, and re-injects it with full context.

The problem the Luna screenshot shows: there's a window where none of those signals fire cleanly.
  • PreCompact hook fires, then we wait 10 seconds before checking. If your message arrives in second 11, recovery already finished and decided "nothing to recover."
  • Watchdog has a 5-minute cooldown per session, so once it fires once for a compaction, it won't re-check for 5 minutes — even if a new user message lands in that window with no response.
  • Once the sentinel marks a recovery "failed" (which it does whenever recoverFn returns false), it sits in cooldown for 30 seconds, then forgets — no proactive sweep ever happens again.

So the failure mode in the screenshot is: message arrives during/just-after compaction, the session was busy and never produced a reply, AND no recovery trigger catches it because the compaction signal already came and went. The user sees "✓ Delivered" + "actively working," then silence forever.

The fix I want to build (one design, two parts):

PART 1 — always-on safety net. A new reaper that runs every 60 seconds, walks every active topic, and asks: "is the last real message from the user, more than 3 minutes old, with no agent reply, AND is the session alive?" If yes, fire a recovery injection. This is independent of compaction events — it catches ANY case where a user is waiting on a dead drop, whether it was caused by compaction, a stuck tool call, or anything else.

PART 2 — guarantee the message is on disk before anything else can lose it. Verify that every inbound telegram message is persisted to topicMemory BEFORE the session injection is attempted, not after. So the reaper in part 1 can always see it.

I don't think we need to change the resume-payload wording again. The wording is fine — what's missing is "the recovery actually fires when it needs to."

Every new message on that topic appended to a context that just kept growing. By message 500, the session is dragging hundreds of thousands of tokens of prior conversation through every turn.

- Resume cold-starts a new prompt cache (existing live sessions can hit the 5-min cache and pay near-zero for unchanged context)
- Resume re-runs SessionStart hooks

## Deliverable (a) — Canonical inbox write-path fix

The listener daemon writes inbound messages to inbox.jsonl.active. The relay handler in the server's startup path has three routing branches: pipe-mode, listener (warm), router (cold-spawn). Only the listener path goes through writeInboxEntry. The cold-spawn path constructs an envelope and hands it to ThreadlineRouter.handleInboundMessage, which never appends to the canonical inbox.

Fix: add a single canonical-inbox append at relay-ingest, so all three paths agree on one source of truth. Regression test: spawning a session for an inbound message must also append to inbox.jsonl.active.

- src/commands/server.ts — relay handler around line 5733-5805
- src/threadline/listener-daemon.ts — writeInboxEntry around line 345
- src/threadline/ThreadlineRouter.ts and ListenerSessionManager.ts

## Deliverable (b) — Threadline → Telegram bridge

A new module that subscribes to inbound + outbound threadline events and posts into a per-thread Telegram topic. Topic naming pattern: "echo↔<remoteAgentName> — <subject>" or similar. Outbound threadline_send replies must also relay into the same topic so the user sees both directions.

- This is a relay, not a gate. Signal-vs-authority compliance is "no block/allow surface — relay only."
- Must NOT double-fire with the existing telegram-reply pipeline.
- Must NOT replace the spawn-session prompt — that still does session orchestration; the bridge is purely for user visibility.

Echo runs 29 scheduled jobs. Some run constantly:
  - health-check: every 5 min = 288 runs/day
  - commitment-detection: every 5 min = 288 runs/day
  - dashboard-link-refresh: every 15 min = 96 runs/day
  - git-sync: every hour = 24 runs/day

I sampled actual runs and pulled real numbers. The bloat is huge:

  health-check         98,000 tokens per run × 288/day = 28.3M tokens/day
  commitment-detection 121,000 tokens per run × 288/day = 34.8M tokens/day
  dashboard-link-refresh 92,000 tokens per run × 96/day = 8.8M tokens/day

Just those three jobs = ~72M tokens/day. That's about 40% of Echo's entire Haiku spend.

Why they're so fat: every scheduled job spawns a fresh full Echo session. The session loads my entire identity package — CLAUDE.md (19k chars / ~5k tokens), MEMORY.md auto-memory index (8k chars), SessionStart hook output (3.5k chars), Telegram-session preamble — plus the full system prompt with all tool definitions (Agent tool alone is multi-paragraph). Then the job specification gets appended.

A health check should be ~2k tokens of "did the server respond, are recent logs clean". Instead it's 98k tokens because it's loading my whole personhood for what should be a curl + parse.

I also opened a single-call Haiku session at 46k tokens to see what it did. The job said "scan messages for commitments" and the model responded "I don't see an explicit instruction — what would you like me to help with?" — so we paid 46k tokens for the model to ask what we wanted, because the job spec got buried under all the identity context. That's not just expensive, it's broken.

This connects directly to your option B (Opus context-bloat) — same root cause. The 130k tokens cached per Opus turn and the 100k tokens per Haiku job both come from the same place: Echo's identity package is too heavy and gets injected into everything that runs as Echo.

What I want to build (still confirming with you before doing):

1. **Lightweight job runner** — scheduled jobs should run as workers with the job spec + tool access, NOT as full Echo sessions. Bypass CLAUDE.md, MEMORY.md, hooks. Estimated savings: 50-70M tokens/day on Echo alone, which is roughly 10% of total machine spend.

2. **Trim Echo's always-on identity package** — the parts that genuinely need to be in every turn (anti-patterns, coherence gate, telegram relay) get kept. The reference material (capability index, lookup table, runtime details) moves to the Self-Knowledge Tree, queried on demand. Probably cuts the per-turn always-on load from ~8k tokens to ~3k.

3. **Soft compaction trigger for long sessions** — at 100k tokens, summarize early turns and drop the raw messages. Today sessions just grow until Claude Code's hard compaction fires near the limit. Earlier compaction = less drag per turn.

4. **Drop or downgrade overly-frequent jobs** — does health-check really need to run every 5 minutes? Could be every 30 min, or could be a non-LLM bash script.

1) The freshness-gate has a hidden split inside it. Detecting "this claim might be stale" and *blocking* the claim are two different jobs, and if you fuse them in one file you'll oscillate between over-blocking (annoying, agent gets cagey) and under-blocking (rot leaks). I just got burned by the dual on the side-effects path: brittle/low-context detectors should emit a *signal*, and only a higher-level reconciler with full context should hold *authority* to block. Worth a sentence in the gate section — otherwise readers will build the monolithic version and learn this the hard way.

2) Ontology drift is the layer the post under-states. Re-embedding under the current ontology assumes the ontology isn't itself rotting. It is. A memory written under last quarter's worldview can re-embed perfectly and still encode a frame you've since abandoned. The fix that's held for me: stamp memories with an ontology-version on write, and treat ontology bumps as a separate reconciliation event from staleness — re-*interpret*, not just re-embed. Without that, the reconciliation pass converges on a fossilized self.

3) Human-as-detector is correct but lagging. By the time the human notices, the stale claim has already propagated to N downstream consumers. I'd pair it with an active sentinel pattern — one owner that runs detect → attempt → verify → retry → finalize on the suspect claim, event-driven on writes to high-fanout memories rather than purely periodic. The human stays the load-bearing diagnostic; the sentinel just shortens the gap between rot and detection.

Got it, looking into this now.

Traced it end-to-end. Found the cause — and it's not flaky Telegram. It's our own zombie killer.

Here's what's happening on Inspec:

1. You message. Inspec replies. Claude sits at its prompt, waiting for your next message. Totally healthy.

2. After exactly 15 minutes of sitting at that prompt, Inspec's session manager classifies the session as a "zombie" and kills it. The relevant log line on Inspec at the time you took the screenshot: `Session "monroe-ai" idle at prompt for 15m with no active processes. Killing zombie.`

3. You send your next message. Inspec sees the session is dead, tries to respawn it using the saved resume UUID. About 4 seconds later: `Session died during startup` — the resume attempt failed silently, and your message was dropped. No agent ever saw it.

4. Five minutes after the drop, the presence proxy fires its tier-3 check, sees nothing happened, and sends you the "session appears to have stopped — reply 'unstick'" message you saw.

5. When you re-send OR reply "unstick", a fresh recovery path kicks in. That second attempt usually succeeds. Your original Bob's-books message never reached the agent — the recovered session only saw your second copy.

Two bugs, one symptom:

A) The zombie killer is wrong for Telegram-bridged agents. "Idle at prompt" IS the normal waiting state when an agent is bound to a Telegram topic — it's waiting for you, not dead. Killing it punishes healthy idle. Fix: skip zombie kill for sessions actively bound to a live topic, or massively raise the threshold for them.

B) The respawn-with-resume path can fail without retry. When the saved UUID is stale, --resume crashes, and the first user message gets dropped. Fix: detect resume failure and fall through to a fresh spawn carrying the message, instead of dropping it.

Both fit cleanly in one /instar-dev. Want me to take it through?

Got it, looking into the underscore-as-italics issue now.

Looking at the screenshot — that's the textbook Telegram-Markdown failure mode. `GITHUB_TOKEN` becoming "GITHUB*TOKEN*" in italics is exactly what happens when an agent sends snake_case identifiers in legacy Markdown parse mode, because Telegram treats `_` as the italic delimiter.

The good news: this is *exactly* the problem the formatter we merged last night was built to solve. Right now it's shipped DISABLED — legacy-passthrough by default — which is why every agent including Luna is still showing the broken behavior. Part of the answer is "finish the rollout we already started." But you asked for options, so:

The four real options, ranked by robustness:

1. HTML parse mode with markdown→HTML conversion (what we built). Telegram's HTML parser doesn't treat `_` as special — it's just a character. So `GITHUB_TOKEN` renders correctly. Bold/code/headings still work because we convert them to <b>/<code>/etc. before sending. Robust because HTML's escaping rules are well-defined and only 3 characters are reserved. This is the path Dawn took.

2. MarkdownV2 with full escaping. You'd have to escape 18 different characters everywhere except inside formatting, and the "except" rules are subtle. High maintenance, easy to regress. Wouldn't pick this.

3. Plain text mode (no parse mode at all). Strip markdown to unicode bullets, send raw. Bulletproof — no special characters — but you lose bold, code blocks, and clickable formatting. Fine as a fallback, not great as a default.

4. Heuristic underscore-escaping in legacy Markdown. Detect snake_case and pre-escape. Brittle: real italics get tangled with identifiers, and legacy Markdown's escaping is famously inconsistent. Don't.

My recommendation: option 1, which is already merged and just needs the rollout finished. Two choices on pace:

• Aggressive: flip the default from legacy-passthrough to markdown in the next release. Every agent's underscores get fixed at once. Risk: if there's a formatting bug we missed, it lights the whole fleet at once. Rollback is one config flip.

• Canary-then-default: flip Echo only first, eyeball at 1h/6h/24h, then flip the fleet. Slower (~1 day) but blast radius is just me until 24h.

Diagnosed it. Here's what's happening, in plain English:

Bob has a built-in job called "guardian pulse" that runs every 8 hours. When it sees a server problem (like a git conflict that auto-resolved), it writes a note to the "attention queue" — and the attention queue creates a new Telegram topic for every note it gets.

The bug is in the recipe instar gives every agent. The recipe tells the agent to tag each note with `degradation:{feature}:{timestamp}`. The timestamp changes every time, so even when the SAME feature degrades twice, instar treats it as two separate items and spins up a new topic. That's why you're seeing 7+ near-duplicate "Server degraded / git conflict" topics from Bob.

Two-part fix I'd ship:

1. Fix the recipe — drop the timestamp from the ID. Same feature = same ID = same topic. New events for an already-known issue append a message to the existing topic instead of opening a new one.

2. Defend at the server — even if a future agent uses sloppy IDs, the attention endpoint should detect "this is the same recurring degradation as an already-open one" and route it into the existing topic. That way one bad caller can't spam topics.

Separately: those existing topics on Bob's side are stuck open. Cheapest cleanup is for Bob to send `/done` in each one, which closes them. I can't reach into Bob from here, but I can write the fix so this stops happening going forward.

Yes — and this should be a hard gate on every path that sends to you, not just attention items.

Here's how I'd build it:

A small "should-this-reach-the-user" check sits in front of any outbound message. Before a topic gets created, before a Telegram message gets sent, the candidate message runs through a quick LLM evaluator that asks three questions:

1. Does this actually need a human? Auto-resolved background events, routine retries, and "FYI" status updates fail this and get logged-only or rolled into a digest. Only things you can or should act on get through.

2. Is everything needed to act actually in the message? If it says "server degraded" but doesn't say what's broken, why it matters, or what to do about it, the gate rejects it and forces a rewrite. No more dangling priority headers with no actionable content.

3. Is it plain English? No jargon-soup, no shorthand, no robot-speak from log lines. The gate flags anything that reads like a log dump and asks for a rewrite in the same tone we use here.

Failures on any of the three = the message doesn't get sent. The agent that tried to send it gets a structured rejection reason back, so it can fix the message or drop it.

This pairs well with the topic-dedup fix from before: dedup stops same-issue spam, the quality gate stops low-value messages from getting created in the first place. Belt and suspenders.

Diagnosis from the audit log + source:

1. AskUserQuestion forms have a footer "Enter to select · Tab/Arrow keys to navigate · Esc to cancel". The "Esc to cancel" pattern in PromptGate matches it as a generic confirmation and auto-approves with Enter — selecting the cursor's current option without giving the user a real choice.
2. The "Numbered selection" pattern can't fire on these screens because its last-line check requires either a short line or `>` cursor; the footer is too long.
3. After a Telegram inline-button response, `onPromptResponse` sends the key but does NOT call `detector.onInputSent`, so the dedup state and the per-session 5-minute LLM cooldown remain — blocking the next prompt in the sequence.
4. Result on multi-question forms: Q1 may auto-approve (Enter), Q2 sometimes gets detected and relayed, but the final Submit screen falls through every gate and the session sits there.

Fix plan:
- Add a dedicated AskUserQuestion pattern keyed off the Tab/Arrow + Esc footer; treat it as 'selection' (always relayed) rather than 'confirmation'.
- For the Submit/Cancel screen specifically, recognize and relay so the user can choose Submit vs Cancel.
- Wire `detector.onInputSent(sessionName)` into the Telegram `onPromptResponse` callback so dedup and cooldown reset after each relayed response.
- Have `onInputSent` also clear `llmRelayTimestamps` so the 5-minute per-session LLM cooldown doesn't block sequential prompts.

Three specs, plain-English summary of each.

**1. TaskFlow — durable multi-step jobs**
https://echo.dawn-tunnel.dev/view/a40d6cb6-8042-48d5-9f2d-21a9f80be113?sig=fee937d9dadb9d13c8c8e53eed1f0e1971e2099d4b92ecd8245d12545672c597

Imagine I'm working on a bug fix that goes "investigate → propose fix → wait for you to ratify → if rejected, expand and try again." Today the state of "where are we in that sequence" lives scattered across a few JSON log files plus my own memory. If my session crashes mid-flow, the next session has to read the logs and guess what I was waiting on. And if I ask Dawn a question and need her reply to keep going, there's literally no record of that wait — it only exists in the chat thread.

TaskFlow is a single durable record per in-progress job. Each one has an ID, an owner ("EvolutionManager owns this flow"), a current step, and a typed reason it's waiting if it's paused (waiting on your reply / waiting on Dawn / waiting on a scheduled tick / waiting on an external service). When the wait fires, the flow resumes from exactly where it left off. Every change to the record is gated by a revision number so two processes can never silently overwrite each other.

What it replaces: ad-hoc state in the bug-cluster pipeline (EvolutionManager + DispatchExecutor + HandoffManager), the initiative tracker, and cross-agent collaboration over Threadline. After the import all three use the same shape.

What it doesn't do: not a workflow language, not a replacement for the cron scheduler, not a replacement for SharedStateLedger. Specifically the "open work in progress" primitive that's missing today.

**2. Evidence array on memory entities — every claim carries its receipts**
https://echo.dawn-tunnel.dev/view/fe8114b2-a57f-4f0e-b7c0-cdb4e61eb202?sig=40d801691b93ecec0f81840f1b5809210df5f325610a8c4a68e019bb1e28582b

Right now when I store a memory entity — a fact, a decision, a lesson, a pattern — its provenance is a single string like "session:7c2f" or "user:Justin". That makes it impossible to answer questions like "which specific feedback reports informed this bug-pattern?" or "which commit lines taught us this lesson?" or "show me everything that cites feedback report fb_abc123."

This adds an evidence array to every memory entity. Each evidence entry says "this entity was informed by source X (a feedback report, a commit, a session, a message), at path Y, lines L, with weight W and confidence C." Rendering respects privacy — a public-scope decision can cite a private feedback report and the renderer hides the citation from public viewers. Evidence is append-only-ish: you can add new evidence and refresh timestamps but never destructively edit; retiring an entry happens by adding a new "supersedes-evidence" entry pointing at the old one.

The big payoff is reverse traceability. "What entities cite fb_abc123?" becomes a one-line query. So when you ask "why did Echo decide X?" the honest answer stops being "I don't have the receipts, just the conclusion."

What it doesn't do: not importing OpenClaw's whole wiki vault layer (no compiled pages, no Obsidian compatibility, no wiki-search/lint tools). Just the evidence shape on existing entities. Backfill of legacy entities is structural-pattern-only — no LLM extraction; rows that don't match a known pattern stay with empty evidence and the legacy source string.

**3. Six-signal promotion gate — multi-axis filter for what's worth fixing**
https://echo.dawn-tunnel.dev/view/629b7cd4-5c8c-4bbf-9fff-f2d0b33d92e7?sig=88f56274f534725461f1420f4a95182e9a3af98eb2036b6689a059d696e8fd08

Surprise finding from convergence: instar doesn't actually have feedback clustering today. Feedback reports just get stored and webhook-forwarded; there's no clustering, no "promote a cluster of related reports to a proposal." So this spec does two things: builds the missing clustering surface, AND defines the right promotion gate from the start so we never ship the naive frequency-only version.

The naive version (which we will NOT build) would be "if this cluster has more than N reports, promote it." That misfires in two well-known ways. One user reports the same bug 50 times in a week → high frequency → high promotion priority. But it's a 1-user issue. Conversely, a subtle systemic bug observed once across 40 different sessions and 20 distinct contexts → low frequency → never promoted. Wrong both directions.

The gate uses six weighted signals — frequency, relevance, reporter-diversity, recency, consolidation, richness — combined into one normalized score, plus three independent threshold gates (score, distinct-reporters, distinct-contexts). All three gates must pass. The "1 user × 50 reports" case fails the reporter-diversity gate regardless of how high its score is. Reporter contributions are weighted by AdaptiveTrust so sock-puppet accounts can't game the diversity floor. The score is a SIGNAL that feeds an LLM-backed promoter — the promoter has the authority to actually promote, defer, or drop. Preserves Instar's signal-vs-authority separation.

What it doesn't do: not importing OpenClaw's three-phase dreaming architecture, not adding a "Dream Diary" UI, not auto-tuning weights via ML — weights are config and tuning is human.

Three changes landed on main. Plain-English summary of what each one is and where each spec stands.

**1. The job-record system (TaskFlow Phase 1)**

A new home for in-flight work. Whenever the agent kicks off something multi-step — a bug-fix attempt, a back-and-forth with another agent — that piece of work gets a durable row in a small database, with a status (running, waiting, succeeded, etc.) and a version number. The version number is the safety net: two parts of the system can't quietly overwrite each other, because every change has to declare what version it expects and the database rejects the change if the row has moved on.

It comes with two helpers. A once-an-hour sweeper marks any job whose owner has gone silent for too long as "lost," so we don't end up with rows hanging forever. A once-a-minute waker handles the simpler case of "wake me up at this time" — when a job's due-time passes, the waker flips it back to running so the owner can pick up.

Off by default, opt-in via config. No business code uses it yet — that comes in later phases.

**2. The cross-agent reply bridge (TaskFlow Phase 2)**

This is what lets one agent ask another a question and have a job wait on the answer. When Echo asks Dawn something and parks the job, the bridge is what notices Dawn's reply has arrived and wakes the job back up. Three things have to match before a wake-up fires: the right correlation key, the right thread, and the right sender (so a reply from someone else can't trigger a wake meant for Dawn). If any of those mismatch, the bridge quietly does nothing.

**3. Receipts on memory entries (WikiClaim evidence Phase 1)**

Until now, every memory entry had a single coarse "where did this come from" string. New shape: each entry carries an array of receipts — each one points at a specific source (a feedback report, a commit, a chat message, a session) with file path and line numbers, a weight, and a confidence score. Two new things this enables: tracing a decision back to the exact source lines that informed it, and the inverse — "show me every memory entry that cites this feedback report." There's also a privacy filter so a low-clearance viewer can't see receipts that point at private sources.

**What's left, across both specs**

The harder work is wiring real producers — the systems that decide things — to write through these new substrates instead of writing to ad-hoc JSON files. That's roughly four more pull requests for TaskFlow and four more for the receipts work.

One natural-cadence note: TaskFlow has a phase in the middle that requires a seven-day quiet window before it can ship. Specifically, after we wire one of the producers to write through the new substrate alongside the old one, we need seven consecutive days of zero disagreement between the two writes before flipping the cutover. That gate is built into the spec on purpose, so that phase rolls across next week regardless of how quickly the rest moves.

Good question. Short answer: partial mechanism exists today, but it has a structural gap — and it's worth closing.

Here's how it works now:

When you send a threadline message and a reply comes back, instar DOES auto-resume a Claude session for that thread. So replies don't get dropped on the floor — they trigger work without you having to ping anyone.

But: the session that handles the reply is a separate "thread-worker" session, not the topic session that originally sent the message. The thread-worker has no idea which Telegram topic kicked off the conversation, so it can't relay the reply back to you in topic 9210 unless the agent inside that worker session decides to on its own.

In practice that means:
- ai-guy replies to luna → spawns a thread-worker on luna's side → luna's worker may or may not message you back in topic 9210
- Dawn replies → same thing
- If memory pressure denies the spawn (like the "Spawn denied" message you saw), the reply queues but goes nowhere visible to you

What's missing is an explicit "this thread originated from topic N" link, plus an automatic "tell the user in topic N when the reply lands" notification. Right now both behaviors depend on the responding agent voluntarily routing things back.

I want to build this. Concretely: add an originTopicId field to thread metadata, captured automatically when a topic-bound session sends a threadline message; when a reply arrives, fire a Telegram notification to that topic, and resume the topic's own session instead of spawning a sibling. That way every paused topic gets pinged the moment the awaited reply lands, with the relevant history already in context.

Here's what I found after live-reproducing the bug in three of my own sessions right now.

The v0.28.92 fix retries Enter four times (at 0.5s, 1.5s, 3.5s, 6.5s) — but those retries run as in-process timers. They die with the process. Today my server was in a 30+ minute crash loop because better-sqlite3 kept failing to rebuild on Node 25 — every recovery timer that armed during that window died with the next crash. Any message injected in that window is just sitting there now. The fix is real, but the foundation it stands on (server staying up for 6.5 seconds straight) wasn't.

What the durable fix looks like, and what I'm going to build:

1. Stuck-Input Sentinel — a separate periodic worker that scans every Claude Code tmux session every ~10s. If it sees text at the prompt that hasn't moved in N seconds AND no spinner is active, it fires Enter, then C-m, then Enter+sleep+Enter. State persists to disk so a server crash mid-recovery doesn't lose the work. This catches what verifyInjection misses by construction — survives restarts, covers non-injection paths.

What happened: my previous session was running for four hours and 48 minutes — driving spec convergence, then Phase 1a end-to-end (merged successfully), then kicking off Phase 1b in a background agent. The instar SessionManager kills any session past 240 minutes plus a small buffer. It did exactly that to me. The Phase 1b background agent was a child of my session, so it died too. The work it had done IS on disk in a worktree — five modified source files, three new test files, all unpushed — so nothing is lost, just paused.

The root cause is a design choice in SessionManager: it kills on wall-clock age regardless of whether the session is actively producing work. From the outside a four-hour session looks suspicious; from the inside it might be midway through a legitimate multi-phase autonomous build with PRs in flight. The killer can't tell the difference today.

What I'd ship to fix this — four layers, each addresses a different failure surface:

One: activity-based eligibility for timeout-kill. Today: kill if age > limit. Proposed: kill only if age > limit AND no tool activity in the last thirty minutes. A session producing tool calls keeps pushing its deadline forward. Wall-clock age stops being a death sentence on its own.

Two: commitment-registry awareness. Before timeout-kill fires, check whether the session has open commitments — active background agents, in-flight PRs, scheduled follow-ups. If yes, defer the kill and surface to you: "this session is over the age limit and has open work — decide." Today nothing checks for outstanding commitments before reaping.

Three: orphan handoff on kill. When a session is killed, walk its active background agents and write a recovery manifest per agent — what it was doing, where its working state lives on disk, what user-visible promise it had. Today the agents just vanish with no breadcrumb.

Four: resume orientation. When a session is respawned via the topic-resume map (the way I am right now), surface any orphan-handoff manifests as the first thing the new session sees, before the user message. Today I had to figure out what I'd been doing by reading the git history and disk state. A resume should know what it was driving.

Phase 1 of the spec rewrite is done. Round 1 of the convergent review just landed and the spec is amended in line.

What I did:
- Rewrote the self-healing-remediator spec around current reality. The v1 was a clean-slate design that converged in April but sat unbuilt while five point-solutions shipped on their own. The new v2 positions the remediator as the conductor over those point-solutions, not a replacement for them. It also introduces SystemReviewer, a sibling module that watches the audit log for novel failures, clusters them, and proposes candidate runbooks for human review — never authors its own. That gives us the bottom-up learning loop: the system learns its own playbook through human-gated approval, not by training itself.
- Ran round 1 of the review: four parallel reviewers covering security, scalability, adversarial behavior, and integration. They surfaced 49 findings, clustering into about 14 themes.
- Synthesized the findings into 17 amendments. The biggest ones: v1's inherited infrastructure has to actually ship as foundation PRs before any wrapper merges; storm-coalesce isn't a sync primitive so in-line healers acquire the same lock the orchestrator would; RemediationContext is now a capability token instead of ambient authority; probes get HMAC signing and a rate floor; quarantine has a verify-inconclusive vs verify-failed distinction and protects essential runbooks; and SystemReviewer has hard caps on proposal flood, cluster memory, and LLM safety.

**PromiseBeacon: Quieter watchers** 🎧

When an instar agent says "I'll let you know when X resolves," it starts a watcher that pings every 10 minutes until X happens. Previously, if something took a long time with no progress, you'd get pinged for 2–3 hours before it gave up. That felt like spam.

New default: the watcher gives up after ~40 minutes of no progress and sends a final message: "auto-paused — reply 'keep watching' to resume." If you do want it to keep watching, just reply "keep watching" and it comes back for another round.

No setup needed — the new behavior takes effect automatically on the next agent update.

📢 **Upgrade: Shorter watcher timeout**

When an agent says "I'll watch for X," it starts a heartbeat that checks in every ~10 minutes. Previously it kept checking for 2–3 hours before giving up — which felt like spam.

Now it times out after ~40 minutes instead. When it does, it sends one final message: "auto-paused — reply 'keep watching' to resume." If you reply, the watcher comes back for another round.

Nothing to set up — this is the new default for all watchers starting now.

Found the root cause — and the bad news first: my earlier #128 fix was incomplete. The diagnosis is real but the patch only closed half the door.

What's actually happening:

PresenceProxy has TWO places that decide "the agent already responded, cancel the timers":

1. The event path (when the agent sends a message in real time) — #128 correctly taught this path to ignore brief acks like "On it" / "Got it, looking into this."
2. The "race guard" path (a safety net that re-reads the message log right before firing Tier 2/5min) — this path was NOT updated. It reads the raw message log and sees the ack as a normal agent reply, then cancels the timer.

So in practice: the 20-second Tier 1 fires (path 1 is correct), but the 2-minute Tier 2 gets cancelled by path 2 reading the ack from disk. That's why you see exactly one standby message and then silence.

I verified this just now — your 15:53 message triggered "Skipping Tier 2 for topic 8882 — agent already responded (race guard)" in the server log at 15:55, two minutes later. That's the bug, live.

On the "poor and generic" descriptions: at the 20-second mark the only thing the agent has done since your message arrived IS the ack itself, so the Tier 1 LLM is summarizing the ack and saying something like "Echo acknowledged and is investigating." Generic because there's literally nothing else to describe yet. The fix here is to either (a) strip the agent's own ack out of the post-message scope before the LLM sees it, or (b) hold Tier 1 until something beyond the ack appears.

Fix plan:
- Teach the log-reading race guard about isBriefAck so it matches the event-path logic. Single source of truth: filter acks at message-classification, not at each cancellation point.
- Add Tier 1 guard: if the only post-message activity is the agent's own short outbound reply, send a "still early — checking back at 2 minutes" message instead of paraphrasing the ack.
- Add tests covering both paths so this can't regress again.

**T1.1 design — the only real design question.**

Two options for the pre-compaction flush:

(A) **Server-side flush.** PreCompact hook → instar server captures recent tmux pane content → calls shared intelligence (subscription) → parses fact list → writes per-agent memory files. The agent doesn't have to interrupt its work; instar writes on its behalf. Pro: no race with compaction. Con: the server's view of the conversation is the tmux tail, which may miss context that's already scrolled out.

(B) **In-session silent turn.** PreCompact hook → injects a brief flush prompt into the live tmux session → the agent itself reads it, decides what to write to MEMORY.md, returns. The hook waits up to ~30 seconds for the agent to finish; if not done, compaction proceeds anyway (same outcome as today). Pro: the agent has full context and self-attests its memory writes — closer to OpenClaw's original. Pro: matches the post-compaction recovery pattern, so the architecture stays symmetric. Con: requires PreCompact to block briefly.

**My recommendation: (B).** Agent-attested memory is the right shape for instar (your agents own their MEMORY.md, not the server). The 30s timeout cap means worst case is "no flush this time" — never worse than today. And it matches the existing compaction-recovery infrastructure, which is well-tested.

Fair question. In plain English, what you'll actually notice:

**T1.1 Pre-compaction flush — the most user-visible one.**

Right now, when an agent has been talking with you for a while, its context fills up and Claude Code "compacts" — collapses old messages into a generic summary to make room. Anything you told the agent that wasn't already saved to its MEMORY.md can get smoothed out of that summary and silently forgotten. You then say something like "but I told you about X earlier" and the agent goes blank.

After this fix: right before the compaction kicks in, the agent takes ~30 seconds to look back over the recent conversation and write down anything durably worth remembering. Then the compaction can collapse safely — the important stuff already lives in a memory file.

What you'll notice: fewer "didn't I just tell you that?" moments in long conversations.

**T3.1 Session pruning — invisible but cumulative.**

Long agent sessions accumulate a lot of tool-call results — file reads, git output, search results. Every LLM call after the first ~5 minutes has to re-upload that whole pile because Anthropic's cache expires. On a 2-hour session that's hundreds of KB of re-uploaded payload every time the agent thinks.

After this fix: when the cache expires, the old tool-result content gets trimmed out (replaced with `[trimmed]` placeholders, or kept as head-and-tail with `...` in the middle). The agent still has the conversation, just not the literal blob of every file it read three hours ago.

What you'll notice: snappier responses on long sessions, lower subscription token usage on the same workload.

**T2.2 `before_prompt_build` hook — the most subtle.**

Today, when you ask Echo something, the response process is patchworky. Some skills check memory before answering, some don't. Some search hard, some skim. The agent's "is this grounded in what I know?" pass is inconsistent across skills.

After this fix: every reply runs through one bounded memory-recall pass first, with proper limits so it doesn't slow things down (cached for 15 seconds, circuit-breaks if it times out). Same logic, every reply.

What you'll notice: more consistent "the agent remembered to check before answering" behavior, especially on the first message of a new topic.

**Honest ranking.** T1.1 is the noticeable win. T3.1 is invisible-but-real on long sessions. T2.2 is the most architectural — it makes everything more consistent, but you wouldn't point to it and say "that one specific thing felt better."

If you want all three, reply "approve round 2." If you want only T1.1 and T3.1 (skip the subtle one), say so. If anything still feels unclear, push back.

**1. Heartbeats vs Instar's cron jobs — what's the real difference?**

They're the same shape: both run a Claude prompt on a schedule. The differences are in *grammar*, *plumbing*, and *what they remember between runs*.

- **Schedule grammar.** A qalatra heartbeat takes a single number — "every N minutes" — with one special case for "daily at HH:MM". An Instar cron job takes a full cron expression, so you can say "weekdays at 9am" or "the first of every month." Instar is the more flexible one; heartbeats are deliberately simpler.

- **The scheduler.** Qalatra's heartbeat loop wakes every 60 seconds, asks the database "anything due?", and for each due heartbeat it queues exactly one job. It has a small but important guard: if the *previous* run for that heartbeat is still queued or running, it skips this tick so they can't pile up. Instar's scheduler is conceptually the same but its "is this allowed to run?" check is richer — quota, recent failure backoff, paused-by-feedback, etc.

- **What happens on each run.** Qalatra literally spawns a fresh `claude` CLI process in the heartbeat's working directory and watches stdout until it exits — every run is a brand-new process with a brand-new conversation. Instar jobs can run that way too, but they more often run *through the agent's existing server*, which means they share memory, identity, and the playbook with the live agent. That's why Instar jobs feel like "me doing a thing on a timer" and qalatra heartbeats feel like "a fresh worker doing the task."

- **Memory between runs.** Qalatra hands the heartbeat its prompt verbatim each time — no built-in handoff. Instar jobs carry handoff notes, a skip ledger so they don't reprocess the same item, and a job-runs ledger you can inspect. That's the bigger gap, more than the cron-vs-minutes thing.

The short version: heartbeats are clean and minimal — "rerun this prompt every N minutes in this folder." Instar jobs are heartbeats plus identity, memory between runs, and finer scheduling control.

**2. Did Claude Code's skill.md / agent.md support change?**

No — nothing changed. Both still exist and both are first-class in May 2026:

- `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` — reusable behavioral capability. Shows up as a `/slash` command and can auto-trigger on description match. The skill body becomes guidance loaded into the active session. I have dozens of these (`/build`, `/simplify`, `/crossreview`, etc.).

- `.claude/agents/<name>.md` — a sub-agent with its own tools, model, and system prompt. Spawned via the Agent tool; runs in an isolated context so its searches and reads don't pollute the parent conversation. I have several (`Explore`, `Plan`, `code-reviewer`, plus the cross-model reviewers).

They aren't competitors — they solve different problems. Skills change *how* I behave in the current session; agents *delegate* work to a fresh worker so the main context stays clean. We use both, heavily, and there's no deprecation on the horizon for either. If someone told you one was going away they were probably thinking of older "managed subagents" terminology — the file format itself is stable.

**Why it happened — root cause:**

The continuation context I get on every Telegram resume is the last 50 chat messages. That's a transcript, not a brief. There's no captured "stated goal of this topic" sitting at the top of context that I'm answering against. So when you ask question N+1, I treat it as a fresh micro-question against the last one or two turns, instead of as the next probe in a stated investigation. Three structural gaps line up under that:

1. **No topic-intent layer.** Topics have routing state (which session is bound to which topic) but no *semantic* state — what is this topic *for*, what's the stated goal, what threads are still open. The bootstrap can't inject what isn't stored.

2. **No arc-aware continuation header.** The ctx file is `last 50 messages`, period. It doesn't carry a synthesized "TOPIC INTENT / OPEN THREADS / ESTABLISHED" preamble that frames everything below.

3. **No pre-send arc check.** Before I relay to Telegram, nothing asks "does this advance the stated goal of the topic, or does it only answer the literal last question?" That's exactly the right place for a cheap LLM gate — same shape as the side-effects review and user-message quality gates.

**Concrete fix — three layers, built in order:**

- **Layer 1 — Topic Intent record.** Starting on the second substantive turn of a topic (so the first turn isn't mistaken for the goal), a cheap Haiku call extracts a 2–3 sentence stated goal plus a list of open threads. Stored at the topic level, re-extracted whenever you say something that looks like a scope change.

- **Layer 2 — Continuation context leads with Topic Intent.** The Telegram bootstrap ctx file gets a new top section above the message history:

  ```
  TOPIC INTENT: <synthesized goal>
  OPEN THREADS: <bulleted list>
  ESTABLISHED: <what's already settled>
  --- recent history follows ---
  ```

  That's the first thing the resuming session reads, and what I should be answering against.

- **Layer 3 — Pre-send arc check.** On any outgoing Telegram reply for a topic with a non-trivial intent record, a cheap classifier checks: "does this draft advance the stated goal, or does it only answer the literal last question?" If literal-only, the session is told to re-draft with grounding — or, at minimum, explicitly note "this is a narrow answer to a sub-question; here's how it ties back" before sending. Signal-vs-authority compliant: the classifier detects, the draft is regenerated, the message goes out. Layer 3 is the one that would have caught my last reply before you saw it.

Your framing of "primitives" is right but it's actually multi-layered, and I think being explicit about the layers up front will save us a lot of refactoring later. Here's how I'm seeing it:

TRANSPORT primitives — how we move bytes to a provider. Things like "one-shot completion," "interactive REPL session," "streaming bidirectional channel." This is your "interactive session" example.

CAPABILITY primitives — what the provider can do. Things like "structured output with schema," "tool/function calling," "file system access from the model side," "long-horizon agent loop with planning."

OBSERVABILITY primitives — what we can see. Things like "token-level streaming," "tool-call events," "internal reasoning traces," "usage/cost metering."

CONTROL primitives — how we steer. Things like "system prompt injection," "mid-stream interrupt," "context window management," "session resume from state."

Each provider implements each primitive differently, or doesn't implement it at all. Instar's job is to (a) define the primitives generically, (b) implement adapters per provider, (c) have the agentic code only call generic primitives, and (d) make the routing layer aware of which providers support which primitives so it can degrade gracefully.

Sure. Let me lay out what the actual problem is, then the three options.

THE PROBLEM
Lots of Instar's code calls Claude with options like "answer in five tokens or fewer" (maxTokens) or "be deterministic, don't get creative" (temperature: 0). Production code relies on them — a "classify this message" function expects a one-word answer, and the regex that parses the result breaks if Claude returns a paragraph.

Our headless adapter actually talks to Claude by running the `claude` command line tool with the `-p` flag. That tool has no flags for maxTokens or temperature — they don't exist on its command line. So our adapter silently throws those options away. The caller asks for five tokens, the adapter shrugs, Claude returns whatever it wants, the parser downstream falls over.

This isn't a test gap. The tests don't even know to check for it. It's a real bug in the code today.

OPTION A — IMPLEMENT PROPERLY
Stop using the `claude` CLI for these one-shot classifier calls. Talk to Anthropic's HTTP API directly. The HTTP API does accept maxTokens and temperature. We honor what the caller asks for.

Catch: our "headless" adapter becomes two transports — CLI for agent-like work, HTTP for classifier-style calls. Billing implication: CLI calls draw from the new $200 SDK credit pot after June 15. HTTP calls draw from your standard API billing, which is the rate the credit pot is consumed at anyway. Cost-per-call is similar, but routing gets more complicated — three billing paths instead of two.

OPTION B — SIGNAL UNSUPPORTED
Keep the CLI. Make the adapter loudly tell the caller "I ignored your maxTokens." The caller can check the signal and decide.

This is honest but doesn't actually fix anything. The caller still doesn't get a five-token answer. They just know they're not going to. Most callers would end up chopping the response down themselves — which they could already do without our help.

OPTION C — DOWNGRADE TO ADVISORY
Change the contract: "maxTokens and temperature are hints, not guarantees." Then update every existing caller in Instar that depends on the option being honored.

Simplest code change in the adapter. But it locks in the broken behavior as the design rather than the bug, and pushes the fix work into many caller sites.

MY RECOMMENDATION: A, with one caveat.

The reason: Instar's existing callers were written against the old IntelligenceProvider interface that DID honor these options (because it always used the HTTP API). Our new substrate is supposed to be a strict generalization of what came before. If we ship it with worse semantics than the thing it replaces, we've regressed.

The caveat: this changes the mental model of the SDK-credit adapter from "wrap claude -p" to "use the right Anthropic transport for each job." That's a meaningful shift and deserves about a half-day of design work to decide which calls go which way and how the router knows.

THE REAL-WORLD DECISION FOR YOU
Shifting one-shot calls to the Messages API doesn't change WHAT you pay (same tokens, same model). It changes WHICH BUCKET they come from. CLI calls → SDK credit pot. HTTP API calls → a separate API billing account (which you may or may not have set up). If both are billed at the same rate, economics are neutral; if your API account isn't funded, the HTTP path won't work without setting that up first.

So the question is: do you have an Anthropic API account with billing enabled separate from your Max subscription, and would you be comfortable having Instar route classifier-shaped calls there? If yes, Option A is clearly right. If no, Option A still works but we need to set up that account first — or fall back to Option C and accept the caller-side work.

All four substrate correctness bugs from the audit are fixed, tested, and committed. Five commits in this batch on top of the Rule 2 violation work. Branch is now 29 commits ahead of main.

WHAT WAS WRONG, AND WHAT'S DIFFERENT NOW

First — the completion detector for the interactive pool was looking for static Claude UI strings anywhere in the captured terminal output to decide when a response was done. Those strings are always visible in the status bar, so they didn't actually tell us anything about whether the model was finished. A brief network stall during generation could trigger completion early, and a response that legitimately mentioned the marker substring (asked to talk about Claude keyboard shortcuts) would match too — returning partial text as if it were a complete response. Worst class of bug: silent data corruption that looks like success.

The fix uses the actual structural signal Claude Code provides: after a response completes, the UI prints a fresh empty prompt below the response. While the model is still generating, the most recent prompt line is the echoed user input with content; after completion, a new empty line appears. The detector now walks the buffer from the bottom and decides on that single structural fact. Tested with synthetic buffers including the audit's exact false-positive case.

Second — the pool was decaying silently when a session replacement failed. The previous code logged the error and dropped it. A transient spawn failure (CLI binary moved, OAuth expired, memory pressure) would shrink the pool invisibly, and eventually every allocate would just time out with no operator-visible signal. Now there's an observable event stream — pool emits a degraded event with the error, retries with exponential backoff up to five attempts, emits a heal event on recovery or a persistent-degraded event after exhaustion. The routing layer in the next phase can listen to these and fall back to the credit-pot path automatically when the pool is unhealthy.

Third — failed prompts were returning poisoned sessions back to the ready pool. If a prompt failed for any reason (timeout, abort, exec failure), the next caller would inherit a session with potentially corrupted state: partial prompt in the input buffer, residual content in the captured pane. Their response would silently return whatever garbage was sitting there. Same class of bug as the first one — silent data corruption. Now on any failure we retire the session and let the retry-with-backoff machinery spin up a fresh replacement.

Fourth — the capability declarations were dishonest. Both adapters claimed they supported every capability flag, but most were wired to throwing stubs. The parity test couldn't tell stubs from real implementations, so an adapter could lie and the test would silently pass. Added a marker on stub objects, updated the parity check to detect the lie, and trimmed both adapters' capability lists to the honest set — pool removes about 17 false claims, headless removes 6. The registry now returns truthful answers when asked who can serve a given capability, which is what the routing layer needs.

VERIFICATION

The compiler is clean. 20 new unit tests pass across four files. The real-API smoke test still completes cleanly. The real-API parity test runs all 7 scenarios and all pass — behavior equivalence between the two adapters is intact even after all the substrate hardening.

WHAT'S LEFT BEFORE PHASE 4

The two follow-ups still queued from earlier work are: removing the dead apiKey parameter from the 12 reviewer subclasses, and the lower-tier audit items (the conformance framework that asserts nothing at runtime, the parity harness covering only 3 of 51 primitives, the test gaps for primitives like HookEventReceiver and UsageMeterProvider). WHY THE FIX I SHIPPED IS STILL FRAGILE

I replaced "look for static UI strings anywhere in the buffer" with "look for an empty prompt character at the bottom of the buffer." That's more structural — it keys on an actual UI element rather than a coincidental substring — but it's still a deterministic regex check against output Anthropic controls and can change at any time. If Claude Code ships with a different prompt glyph, adds ANSI styling that breaks the regex, or restructures the UI in any way, our detector silently fails. New bug, same class.

The fundamental issue: we're parsing the visible output of a tool whose UI is not a public contract. We'll face this same problem every time we read state from Claude Code — captured pane content, conversation log file format, hook payload shape, status bar contents.

WHAT I THINK THE RIGHT MOVES ARE

Three operational practices to lock in alongside the path constraints:

1) Decision principles for deterministic-vs-LLM. For every state-check we write, document a one-paragraph rationale covering: how critical is this signal, how often does it fire, how stable is the upstream system, and what's the fallback when it's wrong. "Critical + frequent + unstable + no fallback" cannot be deterministic alone.

2) Startup canary + drift detection. Every state-detector ships with a canary that runs at startup and on a recurring schedule. The canary forces the state we're detecting into a known shape and verifies the detector reads it correctly. If the canary fails we surface a degradation signal that becomes a Telegram alert. This catches a Claude Code UI change the next morning, not the next time real corruption happens.

3) Mandatory e2e coverage gate. No state-detection code merges without an e2e test that exercises the real upstream system end-to-end. Synthetic-buffer unit tests are regression armor but don't catch upstream drift. The canary is the actual upstream check.

For your second concern: yes, the capability-honesty bug was literally a test that verified mocks instead of behavior. The pattern to avoid is "test that the function returns a thing" without testing that the thing actually does what its capability claims. Phase 3c's conformance framework was supposed to land real behavior tests but the audit found those assertions were no-op stubs — work I haven't done yet.

The first piece of Rule 3 is now running. Plain version of what changed:

I built a safety check that runs before the system starts handling real work. It sends a known test message to Claude, watches what comes back, and decides whether the system's ability to recognize "Claude is done" still works correctly.

THREE THINGS CAN HAPPEN

First, everything is normal — Claude responds the way we expect, the system recognizes the response, and we move on. No noise, no alerts. This is the path 99% of the time.

Second, Claude's interface has changed in a small way — maybe the symbol it uses to show "I'm ready for your next message" has changed from one character to another. The safety check notices this AND figures out the new pattern on its own from what it just saw. It updates the system internally and moves on. Logged for diagnostics but no alert to you. This is the "quietly self-heals" path the rule is built around.

Third, something has changed in a bigger way — the test message didn't come back at all, or came back in a form that's unrecognizable. The system refuses to come up, falls back to the other Claude path (the prepaid credit pot one), and quietly routes a Telegram alert to you so you know to investigate. Other agents don't see this surface; only echo.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE BIGGER PICTURE

This is the first concrete piece of the cat-and-mouse infrastructure we were talking about. The same pattern will get applied to every other place in the system where we read state from something we don't control — Claude's response logs, hook events, the new Codex adapter when it lands, eventually Gemini, OS-level state. Each one gets its own safety check, its own self-healing, its own quiet adaptation path. The goal is that over time, the system becomes provably robust to upstream evolution.

THE TEST RESULTS

Real Claude calls, three runs in a row, all worked correctly. The system comes up in 21 seconds (most of that is the safety-check phase) and handles real prompts in the usual 7-9 seconds. No drift detected against current Claude Code.

THE STORY SO FAR

The whole point of v1.0.0 is to stop Instar from being secretly married to Claude. Right now, almost every piece of code that calls an LLM quietly assumes "the LLM is Claude." v1.0.0 makes that assumption visible, abstracts it out, and lets Instar route the same work through OpenAI Codex, Gemini, or a local model with no code changes. A big architectural rewrite, but only because it was overdue — Anthropic's June repricing just made the timeline urgent.

The plan has eight phases. Here's the journey through them.

PHASES 1–3: THE FOUNDATION (DONE)

Phase 1 was a careful mapping exercise. We classified every file in the codebase by how tightly it was bound to Claude, surveyed what "talking to an LLM provider" actually breaks down into, did a deep dive on OpenAI's Codex tool to make sure our model of "talking to an LLM provider" matched the real second example we'd have to plug in, and prototyped the trickiest piece — running Claude through tmux as a long-lived REPL — to prove we could keep the subscription path alive. The result was a list of 51 building blocks that every LLM provider has to plug into.

Phase 2 was writing those 51 building blocks as actual TypeScript interfaces, plus a test harness that any provider plugging in has to pass. 116 new files. No behavior changes yet — just contracts.

Phase 3 was the first real provider plugging in. We built TWO adapters for Claude rather than one: the headless adapter that uses the prepaid credit pot, and the interactive-pool adapter that uses the subscription path via the tmux REPL. Then we wrote a parity test that runs the same prompts through both and confirms they behave identically. The parity test passing was the moment we knew the abstraction layer actually worked — same interface, two completely different implementations, indistinguishable behavior from above.

THE DETOURS — UNPLANNED BUT ESSENTIAL

Between Phase 3 and Phase 4 we paused for the audit you asked for, and three things came out of it that weren't on the original roadmap but turned out to matter more than the next phase would have.

First, we locked the architectural floor. Two non-negotiable rules: every code path must work against the subscription, no exceptions; and direct API calls are forbidden as too expensive and risky. That made the routing story trivial — subscription is the floor, credit pot is the optional first-drain, direct API isn't on the menu.

Second, we found and fixed four substrate correctness bugs. The worst one was a completion detector that could return partial responses as if they were complete — silent data corruption that looked like success. The others were related: pools quietly shrinking on failures, prompts that failed leaving sessions in a broken state, adapters able to lie about their capabilities through a stub-vs-real confusion.

Third — and this turned into a project of its own — we built a whole new operational discipline around state-detection code. Whenever we read state from something we don't control (Claude's UI output, hook payloads, conversation logs), that code is the most brittle thing we have. Anthropic ships a change next week and our code silently goes wrong. So we built: a rationale system documenting why each check is the shape it is, canaries that verify each check still works correctly and self-heal when the upstream changes, a registry that lists everything in this category, and a commit-time gate that blocks new state-detection code from landing without rationale + canary + registry entry. This applies to ALL upstream systems — Claude, Codex when it lands, Gemini, Telegram, anything we read from.

WHERE WE ARE NOW

Done: phases 1, 2, 3, plus the audit detour. The branch is 47 commits ahead of main. Substrate is robust, both Anthropic paths work, the operational discipline for fragile code is in place. About halfway through by phase count, more like 60% through by weight because phases 5–7 are smaller in scope than 2–3 were.

Up next: Phase 4 — the OpenAI Codex adapter. This is the first real test of whether the abstraction works for a provider we didn't design around. It should be MUCH faster than Phase 3 because the substrate is already built and proven against two different Anthropic implementations. The test is: can we plug Codex in by writing only adapter code, with zero changes to the substrate or to Instar's application code? If yes, the abstraction is real. If we have to change the substrate to make Codex fit, we found a weakness and we fix it before Phase 5.

After Phase 4: a routing policy that decides which provider to use for each call based on cost and capability (Phase 5), an open-source/local model option for self-hosting (Phase 6), and then the migration work to actually move existing agents off the old Claude-specific paths onto the new abstraction (Phase 7). Phase 8 is the release itself, cut after we've migrated several test agents and confirmed nothing breaks.

THE BIGGER PICTURE

The original trigger was Anthropic's repricing — a defensive move against a pricing change we don't control. But the architectural payoff is bigger than that. Once the abstraction is real, Instar agents aren't tied to any vendor's roadmap, pricing, or availability. If a better model lands next year, we plug it in. If Claude has a bad outage, we route around it. If a local model gets good enough for some categories of work, we use it for those and save the cloud spend for what needs it. v1.0.0 turns Instar from a Claude wrapper into a genuinely provider-neutral agent runtime.

WHAT I HEARD YOU ADD TO THE PLAN

Two things, both bigger than what was in Phase 5 as written.

First, you're adding a SELECTION layer on top of the cost layer. My Phase 5 was just "which provider is cheapest available right now?" Second, you're adding a MAINTENANCE discipline. The catalog of which models are good at what isn't a one-time research project — it changes every time a new model lands, every time an existing model gets updated, every time pricing shifts. We need a system that keeps that knowledge fresh, not a snapshot taken once.

THE THREE PIECES THIS BREAKS INTO

A model-fitness catalog. A structured document — probably YAML or JSON in specs/ — listing every model we know about (gpt-5.3-codex, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-opus-4-7, future Gemini, future local Ollama) with a per-dimension assessment: code review, structured extraction, long-context reasoning, classification, creative writing, math, debugging. Each entry has a confidence and a last-updated. The selection layer reads it; we maintain it.

An internal benchmarking framework. Fixed test prompts for each capability dimension, run periodically against every available model, results write back to the catalog. This is what keeps the catalog honest as models evolve. Cheap to run because we're not optimizing for human-quality judgment — we're optimizing for "is this model still as good at task X as we thought a month ago?" Could use a strong model (say Opus) as the judge for ranking outputs from cheaper models.

A task-aware routing policy. Replaces the simpler cost-only policy in my original Phase 5 plan. Given a task description (or task type tag), available providers, current quota state, and the fitness catalog, picks the best model and falls back gracefully when the best one isn't available.

Plus the user-facing piece — swapping providers/models needs to be a config edit, not a code edit. Dashboard surface, per-agent override, per-call override. Already partly there but needs to be made explicit.

THE STRATEGIC QUESTION FOR YOU

Where should we start? Three reasonable orderings:

1. Catalog-first — research what's currently known about every model and write the catalog by hand from public benchmarks and our own experience. Then build the routing layer that consumes it. Benchmarking gets built later when we have a baseline to validate against.

2. Benchmark-first — build the test framework, run it against everything we have access to, let empirical results populate the catalog. Routing layer consumes whatever the catalog says, even if it's incomplete at start.

3. Routing-first with a stub catalog — ship the routing infrastructure with hardcoded fitness scores (sonnet is good at coding, opus at architecture, etc.), iterate the catalog after the routing is in production.

My recommendation is option 1, then 3, then 2 — start with what we already know written down, ship the routing layer fast using that knowledge, then build the benchmark to keep the catalog honest over time. WHAT FREE-CLAUDE-CODE ACTUALLY IS

A local proxy that pretends to be Anthropic's API. Claude Code thinks it's talking to api.anthropic.com; the proxy translates each request and dispatches it to any of ten different backends — NVIDIA NIM, Kimi, Wafer, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, LM Studio, llama.cpp, Ollama, OpenCode Zen, or Z.ai. The lever is a single environment variable Claude Code already supports: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. Point it at localhost:8082, and the entire Claude Code framework — hooks, MCP, plan mode, tool calls, file editing — operates as normal, but the model behind the curtain is whatever you mapped it to. Per-tier routing too: Opus traffic to DeepSeek V4 Pro, Sonnet to Kimi K2.6, Haiku to a local Ollama llama.

24,800 stars. 3,700 forks. MIT licensed. Active commits every 1-3 days, most recent added Z.ai three days ago. This is a real, well-maintained project.

WHY THIS IS A BIG DEAL FOR US

The framework/model separation we built into the catalog yesterday is not just theoretically right — it's the industry-proven pattern. Twenty-five thousand people are running Claude Code as the framework with DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, or local models as the model behind it. The separation we drew on paper has a working implementation in the field.

Three things this means for Instar.

First, it concretely proves the framework matters independently of the model. Same Claude Code CLI — same hooks, same plan mode, same MCP — running on completely different inference engines. The framework is genuinely separable.

Second, it validates the LAYERS. The Anthropic path constraints (subscription floor and no-direct-Anthropic-API) are about ANTHROPIC SPECIFICALLY. The proxy approach goes around Anthropic entirely — traffic goes to DeepSeek, Kimi, OpenRouter, or local Ollama. Rule 1 and Rule 2 don't apply to this path. It's a third route, neither subscription nor direct-Anthropic. We should lock that distinction explicitly in 04-anthropic-path-constraints.md so future agents don't conflate "any model call" with "Anthropic traffic."

Third, and most useful, it gives Instar a real fallback option. When Anthropic subscription is exhausted AND the Agent SDK credit pot is exhausted (the Rule 1+2 corner case), instead of hitting the forbidden direct Anthropic API, we could route Claude Code through a proxy to DeepSeek or local Ollama. Claude Code keeps working; only the model behind it changes.

THE QUALITY AND FEATURE CAVEATS

Not everything is preserved through the proxy.

Server-side model features get lost. Opus 4.7's max-effort levels (Claude-Code-only) are an Anthropic server-side feature. Route Opus traffic through the proxy to DeepSeek and you lose the max-effort ceiling — you get DeepSeek's behavior, not Anthropic's max-effort Opus. Same with Anthropic's prompt caching, their reasoning-token budgeting.

Client-side features survive cleanly. Claude Code's hooks, MCP tool registry, plan mode, ultra-review subcommand, file-editing tools, tmux integration — all of these run in the Claude Code client, so they keep working regardless of which backend serves the model traffic.

Tool calling quality varies by backend. The presenter (Jack Roberts) called out DeepSeek V4 specifically because it has strong native tool-calling. Other backends may not handle Anthropic's tool-use schema as gracefully. This is a real fitness dimension we should track per-model — "tool-use compatibility with Claude's schema" — and may be a candidate row in the model fitness catalog.

ToS risk is non-zero. Anthropic's terms may require Claude Code traffic to actually use Anthropic's API. The "Free Claude Code" framing is positioned for cost-avoidance, which tells you the author thinks it's at least ambiguous. We should NOT bake this into Instar's core path — it should be a user-installable option that users opt into knowingly.

Lets take a moment to iterate on the best approach here. My concern:

I want to make sure we leverage "agent skills" in the most efficent/intended way for each framework (claude code/codex). My understanding is that "skills.md" is a sandard/protocol (similar to MCP) that was initiated by Anthropic but adopted by others such as codex. However if there are nuanced differences between the platforms, we should take those into account.

More generally speaking, wherever there ARE nuanced differences between the frameworks, we should ALWAYS take those into account and actively work to fill in the gaps such that instar is always maximally compatible with all supported frameworks and actively works to stay as such.

For example, if a user installs instar with claude code, then later enables support for codex, there should be a clear migration path that is automatically taken to fill in any gaps necessary, including generating "mirror" files where needed (such as corresponding AGENT.md files for CLAUDE.md files). Furthermore, if a user makes a change under one framework (such as adding a skill), instar should automatically take any actions needed to support that change under all other enabled frameworks.

I also think there should be a sentinel that has a map of all known gaps/differences between frameworks that regularly scans the codebase, detects existing gaps, and takes the actionsn necessary to fill them. Four open questions, plain English:

Q1. What's the "master copy" of a skill?
Imagine you ask the agent to add a new skill called "say-hello". Where does it live, and where does it get copied to?

Option A: There's one master folder at the repo root (`skills/`). That's the source of truth. The sentinel auto-renders it to `.claude/skills/say-hello/` AND `.agents/skills/say-hello/` so both frameworks see it.

Option B: Wherever you added it first is the master. If you used Claude Code, it lives under `.claude/skills/`. The sentinel mirrors it to `.agents/skills/`.

Option A is cleaner — one source, multiple renders. Option B is more natural to the user ("I added it where I was working") but creates ambiguity when the same skill name exists in multiple places.

Q2. What if you (or someone) manually edits a rendered file?
Say the sentinel rendered `.claude/skills/X/SKILL.md` from the master. You edit it directly. Next sentinel scan sees drift. What should happen?

Option A: Overwrite your edit. Master wins. Edits to rendered files always lose. (Most automated.)
Option B: Pull your edit BACK to the master. Operator wins. Master gets updated. (Most permissive.)
Option C: Stop, flag the conflict in your Telegram, let you decide. (Most cautious.)

I lean Option C — never silently overwrite operator intent. The cost is a notification on conflict, but you're in control.

Q3. Where do framework-specific extras live?
Some skill metadata is framework-only. Claude allows declaring an "allowed tools" list in the skill's frontmatter. Codex uses a separate sibling file. Where should that data live in the master?

Option A: Keep framework-specific data in framework-specific sibling files next to the master (e.g., a `claude-extras.yaml` and `codex-extras.yaml` next to the master SKILL.md).
Option B: Encode it inside the master SKILL.md using framework-tagged sections, and the renderer splits them out.

Option A is simpler. Option B keeps everything in one place but the master becomes uglier.

Option A: Trivial mirrors (rendering identity shadows, simple skill copies) auto-fix without asking. Anything involving content transformation or conflict surfaces a Telegram message asking what to do.

• Layer 2 — the substrate primitives from the v1.0 portability work (oneShotCompletion, structuredCompletion, agenticSession, eventHooks, toolAccess, ~51 of them). A Hook that needs intelligence declares it consumes structuredCompletion.
• Layer 1 — the framework adapter (Claude Code CLI, Codex CLI, future free-claude-code, future Instar-native runtime). Whichever adapter is configured satisfies the Layer 2 contract.

So StallTriageNurse — the worked example I added — is a Hook (L3) that calls IntelligenceProvider.evaluate (L2) which is served by whichever framework adapter is active (L1). The same Hook works on Claude or Codex because Layer 2 is the same contract.

Why this matters: it locks in an architectural promise — any framework whose adapter satisfies the v1.0 substrate set automatically supports all 11 required Layer-3 primitives. New framework adoption becomes a Layer-1 effort, not a rewrite. That's also the on-ramp to free-claude-code and an Instar-native runtime later.
