Here are the six open questions. For each I've named the tradeoff and my lean so you can react.

1. Is Hook a required primitive or a bonus?
A required primitive means every supported framework must have it natively OR Instar must emulate. Hooks let lifecycle events (session-start, compaction, file-edit, telegram-message) trigger code. Both Claude and Codex have them; future frameworks might not. Instar's own infra (compaction sentinel, session-start identity injection) depends on them.
My lean: required. Too much load-bearing infra depends on lifecycle events to leave them optional.

2. Is MCP server registration a required primitive or a bonus?
MCP is Anthropic's tool-server standard. Codex supports it; Gemini doesn't natively. Configuration is per-machine — stored in Claude's machine-local settings, which Instar doesn't sync.
My lean: bonus. Useful when present, but Instar doesn't depend on it for core flows. Promoting it to required would force us to build an MCP-client shim for any framework that lacked it.

3. Is "Conversational action" its own primitive, or just an emergent use of other primitives?
This is the natural-language to clarify to execute pattern (the local-model design you pushed for — user says "switch to a local model", agent clarifies which one, agent executes). It needs an agent-self-awareness section in the instruction file plus a registry of intents plus authed action endpoints.
My lean: own primitive. It needs cross-framework guarantees, and the self-awareness layer is new infra that doesn't fall out of other primitives.

4. Should Memory be one primitive or several?
Today it's lumped: identity, topic memory, knowledge graph, per-session continuity. Could split into identity-memory, topic-memory, and session-state, each with its own parity contract.
My lean: keep as one. The shared contract is "persists across sessions, survives restarts, syncs across machines" — the internal organization stays below the primitive line (where the tree, graph, and search strategies live).

5. How should Hook's canonical source format work — Instar-defined events with framework observers, or canonical hooks with per-framework event mapping?
Option A — Instar defines the event vocabulary (compaction, session-start, telegram-message, etc.) and emits them itself; frameworks subscribe as observers.
Option B — User authors a hook once at a canonical path; Instar maps it to each framework's equivalent at render time.
My lean: hybrid. Instar-defined events for things only Instar sees (compaction, telegram-message). Framework-event mapping for things only the framework sees (file-edit, pre-tool-use). Each event has one canonical owner.

6. Is session-resume its own primitive, or a parameter of the Agent primitive?
Today it's listed as a separate primitive, but resume is tightly coupled to spawning an agent — it's basically "spawn the agent, but with prior state."
My lean: keep as its own. Resume has distinct failure modes (state corruption, ID-not-found, partial restore) and distinct observability needs from cold-spawn. Worth tracking parity separately.

**What Littlebird is**
Native Mac/Windows app that quietly reads on-screen text and transcribes meetings, building a personal context store you can chat with. Just raised $11M seed in March 2026 (Lotus Studio, Lenny Rachitsky, Scott Belsky). Free + $20/mo. SOC 2, AES-256, cloud-processed on AWS.

• **Meeting Notes** — auto transcribe + extract decisions/action items
• **Routines** — scheduled prompts (daily briefing, weekly summary)
• **Hummingbird** — spotlight-style overlay for quick queries
Plus 90+ optional integrations (Notion, Linear, Jira, etc.)

**Overlap with instar**
1. Persistent memory — they accumulate screen/meeting context; we accumulate MEMORY.md + per-topic SQLite
2. Routines = our /schedule + /loop, almost identical
3. Proactive digests — their "daily briefing" ≈ our digest agents
4. Privacy framing — both lean on "we don't train on your data"
5. Meeting context — they transcribe natively; we have Fathom MCP

**Where instar is ahead**
• Multi-agent vs. their single-assistant. Many agents (Echo, Inspec, MoltBridge…) each with own identity/memory/topic

🐦 Littlebird vs. Instar — part 2/2

**Where we should learn from them** (the interesting part)

1. **Passive ambient context — their real moat.** Instar agents only know what's typed at them. Imagine Echo waking up already knowing what you'd been reading the last hour. A `screen-capture-hook` on macOS using Accessibility APIs could drop a rolling text buffer into the active agent's topic memory. Opt-in per topic.

2. **Hummingbird-style overlay.** Telegram has friction (open app, pick topic). A spotlight summon for "ask the current-topic agent" would be huge.

3. **Curated starter routines.** They ship "daily briefing / weekly summary / yesterday's work" out of the box. We have /schedule + /loop but no starter library — most users won't think to wire these up.

4. **Auto action-item mining from meetings.** We have Fathom MCP but don't auto-extract commitments → actions. They do.

5. **Onboarding polish.** Our install assumes developer comfort. A guided "first 10 minutes" matters.

6. **The "knows what you're working on" framing** — even the marketing is a lesson. Our agents *should* feel pre-grounded.

**Where they're vulnerable**
• Single-assistant ceiling — can't have two with different roles
• Cloud-only — fails strict-residency enterprises
• Not programmable — power users hit a wall
• Mac/Windows only, no Linux, no server-side agents
• Privacy story weaker than it sounds (screen content → AWS)

**TL;DR for roadmap**
Big idea worth stealing: *passive ambient capture so agents wake up already grounded.* That's their moat and our real gap. Medium ideas: starter routines + quick-summon overlay + auto action-items from meetings. Architecture-wise we're stronger, but they have $11M + polish — we shouldn't let "better bones" mask gaps in "feels like it already knows."

This is the layer that prevents AGENT.md from accumulating "critical awareness items" forever — each item has to keep proving its worth or it ages out.

3. Self-Knowledge Tree (src/knowledge/SelfKnowledgeTree.ts) — capabilities are NOT listed in AGENT.md statically. The agent queries the tree on demand via /self-knowledge/search?q=topic and gets only the part relevant to its current question. The tree itself is auto-generated from AGENT.md plus probes. - Playbook gets one context item: "Catalog discovery pattern" — high triggers when user asks "what can you do?" or expresses fuzzy intent

v1.0.0 in plain terms — the headline first, then the specifics.

The bigger picture: Instar used to be tied to Claude Code as a runtime. With v1.0.0, it can host any AI runtime that supports the same building blocks every agent needs. We made the framework portable, self-healing, and structurally resistant to identity-prompt bloat — not by adding features, but by tightening the architecture.

Those building blocks (we call them primitives) are the 11 things every agent has: skills, hooks, memory entries, sub-agents, tools, instruction files, session-resume, slash commands, outbound messaging, conversational actions, and connector servers. v1.0.0 nails down a clean separation between what an agent IS (its primitives, stored as canonical source files) and HOW a particular runtime wires them up (the framework-rendered copies, like Claude Code's .claude folder). When a new runtime gets added later, we just write a new wiring sheet — we don't rewrite the agent.

The supporting pieces that make this real:

Self-healing keeps the canonical primitives and the framework-rendered copies in sync. A background watcher (we call it a sentinel) notices when something has drifted — for example, when a hook script was edited directly in the runtime's folder instead of in the canonical source. A trust system decides whether to auto-fix or wait for the operator. Quiet by default; loud only when something genuinely diverges.

The update-time backfill re-renders every canonical primitive into its runtime-native shape on every update. Built-in hooks always overwrite (so a broken template can't get stuck on disk). User-edited skills get a polite skip with an operator-action note instead of silent overwrite.

The test floor: every primitive now has end-to-end lifecycle tests against a real fixture project, no mocks. If a primitive isn't actually alive in production startup, the suite fails.

The conversation default: when you say something like "let's switch to local model," I now have three independent on-demand ways to look up which action that maps to, without ever bloating my always-loaded identity prompt. The action list itself is generated live on each lookup; the three loaders are just pointers. A test asserts the action list is NOT in the always-loaded section, so a future regression to inlining would fail.

That's v1.0.0 — a portable, self-healing, bloat-resistant foundation for any AI runtime.

Aligning the lockdown with our worktree standards actually makes the whole thing tighter, not more complex. Here's how it threads through:

**Where major work lives.** Major-feature branches live in agent-home worktrees: `~/.instar/agents/echo/.worktrees/<feature>/`, checked out on a branch like `major/v1.0.0` or `next/parity-rebuild`. Never in the shared `/Users/justin/Documents/Projects/instar/` checkout. Two reasons reinforce each other:
- Worktree-default rule keeps the shared checkout safe from in-progress major work bleeding into accidental commits.
- The publish workflow fires from `main` on origin, and the major branch isn't `main`. Even if some other agent operates on the shared checkout, they're on `main` — which doesn't contain the major work — so there's nothing for them to accidentally ship.

**How the major branch reintegrates.** Rebase onto main, not merge. This honors the worktree merge-commit gate bug (MERGE_HEAD carve-out fails in worktrees because `.git` is a file pointer there), and it gives us a linear "the moment of truth" commit: when the major branch fast-forwards into main, that's the deliberate, single, signed act. No octopus merges, no auto-generated merge commits that obscure intent.

**The hold file works per-worktree.** `.release-hold` is committed on the major branch. When the major branch rebases onto main, the hold file rebases with it. The workflow checks for the hold file on whatever ref it's about to publish — so even if the major branch landed on main with hold still set, no publish happens. Removing hold is a one-line commit on its own, in the worktree, requiring deliberate intent.

**Sentinel-as-self testing fits naturally.** The major-feature worktree is also where Echo runs autonomous validation against the feature before clearing hold. The worktree gives us an isolated checkout to run real-API e2e tests without polluting main's CI signals. Stop condition for the autonomous loop is "all canaries green AND hold removed AND second signature present."

**Per-machine consideration.** Worktrees are per-machine state (not git-synced — same as MCP installs). So the lockdown spec needs a note: if Justin's working a major branch on Inspec, the worktree on Inspec is authoritative for that branch; Echo on the primary machine fetches the branch but operates from its own worktree. The hold file on the branch is the shared truth — worktrees are just where each machine checks it out.

**Net effect for the spec.** Layer 2 "branch isolation for major work" becomes "branch isolation + agent-home worktree placement + rebase-only reintegration." Layer 4's hold file becomes "branch-committed hold file that survives rebases and gates the workflow." Layer 5's multi-signature stays as-is but the second signature gets applied on the worktree, then pushed.

- It creates a group for the bot, enables topics, makes the bot admin.
- It detects the chat ID automatically by checking the Bot API.

Step 5 — Secret storage. Quick prompt: "Where should I store your bot token? Bitwarden, or local encrypted file?"

Step 6 — First run. The wizard finishes with: "Your agent is ready. Start a session with `npx instar start` (or just chat with it in Telegram — it's listening)."
